vignette:
Kwame is a 19-year-old African American man who recently began seeking help after months of trying to keep his life tightly controlled and silent. He works as a detective, an identity he had taken pride in for its discipline and composure, but the event that now follows him began when he was taken and held captive during the course of his work. He has great difficulty putting what happened into language. In session, when he tries to describe that period, he stops, rubs his hands together, and says he knows exactly what happened but cannot find words that fit it. What comes across instead are fragments and sensory pieces: being confined somewhere he could not leave, the closeness of other people, the sense of waiting for something terrible to happen, and above all the sounds. Even now, when the memory presses in, he does not always see clear images first. Sometimes he hears it again in his head-the voices, the movements nearby, the noises from the place where he was held-and the sound alone is enough to make his body tense as if he is back there.

In the period immediately afterward, Kwame returned to daily life with the determination to act as though nothing had changed. He told himself that thinking about it would only make it worse, so he worked hard to push it away whenever it started to come up. If a thought appeared unexpectedly, he would cut it off, distract himself, turn to work, music, his phone, anything that would not let the memory gather shape. This effort gave him a sense of control for short stretches, but it also meant that he never spoke about the captivity in any sustained way, even with people close to him. When his girlfriend asked what had happened, he would say only that it was "bad" and then go quiet. What unsettled him was that the event did not return as a story he could tell from beginning to end. It arrived as pieces he could hear, or as sudden waves of fear and dread with no picture attached. At times he would be sitting at home or riding in a car and be hit by the same emotional force he had felt while trapped, his chest tightening and his mind racing, even though he could not immediately call up a full image of the place.

As the weeks passed, night became something he organized his life around. Because the captivity had unfolded in darkness and uncertainty, being outside after dark now feels dangerous in a way he cannot easily shake. He has come to avoid going out at night whenever possible. If an errand can wait until morning, he waits. If friends suggest meeting in the evening, he declines or invents another reason. This has begun to interfere with his work as a detective, where late shifts, evening follow-ups, and nighttime scene visits are ordinary parts of the job. He has tried to trade duties, linger over paperwork, or find reasons to stay inside the station when others head out after sunset. He is aware that colleagues have noticed. At 19, he is already sensitive to being seen as inexperienced, and he is deeply uncomfortable with the possibility that others may read his hesitation as weakness.

Physical contact has also become difficult. Any form of touch can make him recoil before he has time to think. The reaction is strongest when he is caught off guard. A hand on his shoulder at work, someone brushing past him in a hallway, even the casual closeness expected in a relationship can make him go rigid. With his girlfriend, this has become especially painful. He cares about her and does not want to hurt her, but he finds himself pulling away from hugs or stiffening when she reaches for him. He struggles to explain why. He does not have words that satisfy him, and the more he cannot explain it, the more isolated he feels. She has at times taken his distance personally, and he has felt both guilty and cornered, wanting closeness and dreading it at the same time.

By the time he sought treatment, Kwame was exhausted by the effort of staying ahead of his own mind. He was still trying hard not to think about the captivity, yet the sounds of it kept intruding, and the emotional force of it kept appearing without warning. He was avoiding the dark, avoiding touch, and saying less and less about what had happened because language seemed to fail him whenever he approached it. What finally brought him in was the growing sense that his world was narrowing: work after dark was becoming harder to manage, and his relationship was beginning to strain under all the things he could not explain. What frightens him most is the feeling that the event can seize him without an image, without words, and that he may never be able to talk about it clearly enough for anyone to understand. What he hopes for, cautiously, is not to erase what happened but to be able to be outside at night, to be touched without flinching, and to speak about the captivity without feeling swallowed by it.
